title: Advent: waiting
hook: four weeks of candles and longing before Christmas

segments.voice: Yesterday, the liturgical year, and your line: time can be holy. Today, the place the circle begins.

Think about the last time you really waited for something. A baby due any day. Test results. A plane landing with someone you love on it. You can't make it come faster, and you can't stop looking at the door. Now picture an evergreen wreath on a kitchen table in December, with four candles. On the first Sunday, one candle is lit. The next week, two. Then three. Then four. Outside, the nights keep getting longer. Inside, the light slowly grows. The shops have played Christmas songs since early November, but in many churches the songs are still about the dark, and about longing. Today's word is the name of that waiting.
screen: `WAITING AT THE DOOR.` → `FOUR CANDLES, ONE A WEEK.` → `THE LIGHT SLOWLY GROWS.`

segments.voice: Advent, from the Latin adventus: a coming, an arrival. It's the four Sundays before Christmas, and in Western churches it's where the church year begins. Advent looks two ways at once. Back, to the first coming, the birth in Bethlehem, and the centuries of hoping before it. And forward, to what Christians call the second coming, when they believe Christ will return and set the world right. So the readings are full of prophets. Isaiah: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light." John the Baptist in the desert, telling everyone to get ready. The mood is purple: hope, with an ache in it. Many churches sing the old hymn O Come, O Come, Emmanuel, which sounds more like a plea than a party. The wreath is younger than people think. It's usually traced to a Lutheran pastor in nineteenth-century Germany who made a wheel of candles to help the children in his care count down the days. Many wreaths now have three purple candles and one pink, for the third Sunday, when the mood turns toward joy; some add a white one in the middle for Christmas Day. Orthodox Christians keep a longer season before Christmas, a forty-day fast. And the whole thing ends with the Bible's own last prayer, in Revelation: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Advent says waiting isn't wasted time. For Christians it's a kind of prayer: keeping the door open, and the light on.
screen: `ADVENTUS: A COMING.` · `BACK TO BETHLEHEM, FORWARD TO THE END.` · `A WREATH, ONE CANDLE A WEEK.` · then, large: `EVEN SO, COME, LORD JESUS.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and it's safe, light it; if not, turn on one small lamp or just picture a flame, then leave the phone alone and watch the light, noticing how hard it is to wait for nothing in particular. If you pray, say the old line, "Even so, come, Lord Jesus," once, and wait some more. If you don't, let yourself notice what you're longing for.
Advent. From the Latin for coming. Four weeks of waiting and longing before Christmas, where the church year begins. Today's word.
Your line: come, lord. Four candles, lit one week at a time. One hundred ten days, and counting.

notes: Advent wreath origin: commonly attributed to Johann Hinrich Wichern (Rauhes Haus, Hamburg, 1839). Stated without the name; confirm.
Candle colors (three violet and one rose for Gaudete Sunday; sometimes a white Christ candle; some use blue): customs vary. Confirm.
Orthodox Nativity Fast: forty days, from November 15 (civil calendar varies by church). Confirm.
Revelation 22:20 called 'the Bible's own last prayer': it is the last petition before the closing benediction (22:21). Confirm the phrasing.
Adventus used for an imperial arrival: standard background. Confirm.
'Even so, come, Lord Jesus' is offered as a real scripture line 'if you pray', not a new prayer.
